content_list.content_text: African cinema in the 1970s and 1980s witnessed an explosion of invention and creativity that rivaled any other cinematic renaissance the world has seen before or since. Directors were energized by the opportunities, the energy and the politics of the postcolonial era to create increasingly singular and ambitious films. Yet, compared with the films of the French New Wave, they seem underrated today.

Often referred to as "the father of African film," Senegalese writer and director Ousmane Sembène (1923-2007) embodied the new urgency of postcolonial Africa. In 1947, Sembène moved to France, where he worked as a docker in Marseille, joined the Communist Party and became a militant trade unionist. His cinema showed the same political and social engagement he embraced in his life, and his inspired debut came with La noire de... (Black Girl, 1966), the first feature by a Black African to gain international recognition.

information.contentText: The film satirizes corruption in post-independence African governments; El Hadji's impotence symbolizes the failure of such governments to be of any use.

content_list.content_text: Unique among the emerging directors of the 1970s was Senegal's Djibril Diop Mambéty (1945-1998), whose debut feature, Touki Bouki (1973), captured the voice of African youth and brought a dazzling, experimental touch to African cinema. Writer Manthia Diawara wrote that it "tears through the screen with fantasies of African modernity as never seen before in cinema," and critic Mark Cousins described it as "the African equivalent of Easy Rider (1969) or À bout de souffle (Breathless, 1960)." The film also has a political edge, following a young couple who dream of leaving Senegal and embark on a series of adventures to get the money they need, but who decide, at the last minute, that they cannot leave their homeland.

Inspired by the example of Sembene and also by the creation of two major African film festivals - Carthage, in Tunisia, in 1966, and Fespaco (the Panafrican Film and Television Festival), in Burkina Faso, in 1969 - there was a palpable sense of promise surrounding African cinema at the dawn of the 1970s. Electrified by writers such as Frantz Fanon, who argued in The Wretched of the Earth that national liberation would only be possible after the psychological liberation of individuals, the early 1970s saw pioneering directors such as Med Hondo (b. 1936), from Mauritania and based in Paris, go beyond simply imitating Western films to arrive at a cinema with a distinctly African voice that addressed the issues affecting its people.

quote.quote: Visually stunning, Yeelen is the most mystical and the most beautiful of African films.
quote.author: IMDb on Yeelen

content_list.content_text: In East Africa, Mirt sost shi amit (Harvest: 3,000 Years, 1976) by Ethiopian Haile Gerima (b. 1946) was a landmark, a furious and formally radical denunciation of the oppression suffered by Ethiopia's peasants at the hands of landowners, with characters who symbolized the relationship between Africa and the West. At the same time, in North Africa, filmmakers such as Tunisian Abdellatif Ben Ammar (b. 1943) were also producing challenging films, such as the award-winning Aziza (1980). Chronique des années de braise (Chronicle of the Years of Fire, 1975), by Mohammed Lakhdar Hamina (b. 1934), portrayed Algeria's struggle to free itself from French colonial rule. The film created a new awareness of Algerian cinema, winning the Palme d'Or at the Cannes Film Festival.

information.contentText: It is filmed in the Bambara and Fula languages and is based on a legend told by the Bambara people. Although the era is undefined, it is presumably set in the 13th century in the Mali Empire, and it is a heroic quest narrative with magic.

content_list.content_text: If Western and Asian cinema have their roots in literature and theater, African directors found inspiration by looking to the African tradition of oral storytelling. Films such as Hondo's documentary Soleil O (1973), about immigrants in France, and Emitaï (1971), about the conflict between the French army and Senegalese villagers at the end of World War II, employed key devices of that tradition, such as flashbacks and out-of-sequence narratives.

Following in the footsteps of Sembene and Hondo, directors emerged from all over sub-Saharan Africa, people like Ababacar Samb-Makharam (1934-1987), director of Kodou (1970), or Safi Faye (b. 1943), also from Senegal, who became the first woman film director in sub-Saharan Africa with the feature Kaddu Beykat (Letter from My Village, 1975), a docufiction told through a letter narrated by Faye herself. The film is set in the village where Faye was born in Senegal and focuses on the daily life and customs of its inhabitants, while also telling the story of a young couple who want to marry but cannot - because a drought has ruined his crops, the man cannot pay his bride's dowry. With independence still recent and postcolonial governments across Africa sinking into corruption, the focus of 1970s African cinema tended to remain on the present.

information.contentTitle: Scenes from Chronicle of the Years of Fire
information.contentText: During its screening at the Cannes Film Festival, Mohammed Lakhdar-Hamina received death threats from the pro-French Algeria OAS. Michel Poniatowski, the Interior Minister at the time, sent security guards to protect Lakhdar-Hamina and his three children who were attending the festival.

content_list.content_text: The films of this period covered a range of controversial and topical subjects. Sembène's Xala (1975) was cut by Senegalese censors because of its scathing commentary on the new post-independence elites, who had simply replaced the abuses of the colonial rulers with abuses of their own. The ambitious Ceddo (1977), although set in the 19th century, had a clear message to convey about contemporary Africa by telling the story of African traditions under threat from outside forces.

The lyrical Muna Moto (1975), by Jean-Pierre Dikongué-Pipa (b. 1940) of Cameroon, followed Kaddu Beykat in criticizing the system of putting a price on brides. And an important new voice emerged with director Souleymane Cissé (b. 1940) of Mali, who, like Sembène, had studied in Moscow. Cissé's second feature, Baara (Work, 1978), explored the daily lives of workers at a textile factory in Bamako and revealed Cissé's Marxist background in its portrayal of an engineer who challenges the factory owners. The film won the top prize at Fespaco, as did his next one, Finyé (The Wind, 1982), which dealt with class and generational conflict and showed students who dared to challenge the authority of the military government.

quote.quote: I argue that Xala evokes two problematic binary oppositions: between the corruption and decadence of foreign influence and the purity and morality of African tradition, the former represented as 'corrupt' and the latter as 'redemptive'; and between strong, revolutionary 'masculine' women and 'feminine' men: villains and weaklings.
quote.author: Aaron Mushengyezi on Xala

content_list.content_text: If contemporary reality and its themes dominated African cinema in the 1970s, the following decade saw its directors turn their gaze to the precolonial past in search of inspiration. This shift gave rise to a slower-paced cinema, rooted more specifically in African myths than in the furious statements of the previous decade. The conditions for this came from Burkina Faso, a small West African country. As host of the Fespaco festival, it had already had an impact on African cinema out of all proportion to its status as one of the poorest nations on the continent.

However, in the early 1980s, with the support of the nation's young and charismatic leader, Thomas Sankara, the country began producing films that had a crucial influence on the development of African cinema. Wend Kuuni (God's Gift, 1982), by Gaston Kaboré (b. 1951), was the great landmark. Set in the precolonial era, it revolves around a mute boy found alone in the bush and adopted by villagers. Kaboré's next film, Zan Boko (1988), implicitly criticized the political situation in Burkina Faso at the time. Kaboré inspired other directors, among them his fellow countryman Idrissa Ouedraogo (b. 1951), who made his own "village" films, including the acclaimed Yaaba (1989), in which a 10-year-old boy befriends an elderly woman who has become an outcast.

information.contentTitle: Trailer do filme A Viagem da Hiena
information.contentText: Based on his own story and screenplay, Djibril Diop Mambéty made the film on a budget of $30,000 - obtained partly from the Senegalese government. Although influenced by the French New Wave, Touki Bouki displays a style all its own. Its camerawork and soundtrack have a frenetic rhythm, unusual for most African films - known for their often slow, linearly unfolding narratives.

content_list.content_text: The most celebrated African film of the 1980s also follows the example of Wend Kuuni. With the extraordinary Yeelen (1987), Souleymane Cissé left behind the contemporary realism of Baara and Finyé and told a story of myth, magic and ritual set in 11th-century Mali, based on tales passed down through oral tradition. The film has some of the most beautiful cinematography in world cinema. Other notable African films of the period include Med Hondo's epic Sarraounia (1986). In this historical drama, Hondo immortalized one of the few African tribal leaders to oppose French expansionism - Sarraounia, of the Azna - who in 1899 fought the better-equipped colonial military forces with guerrilla tactics.

Hondo's film was acclaimed by critics and won the top prize at Fespaco. The 1980s also saw the arrival of a new generation from sub-Saharan Africa, among them the great Malian director Cheick Oumar Sissoko (b. 1945), whose first feature, Nyamanton (The Garbage Boys, 1986), portrays the lives of street children in Bamako. In Burkina Faso, S. Pierre Yaméogo (b. 1955) also emerged as a name to watch.

information.contentText: The film was shot on 16 mm black-and-white film. It used nonprofessional actors and was shot in the midst of a civil war following the overthrow of Haile Selassie.

content_list.content_text: These talents ensured that African cinema remained a vital presence on the international scene during the 1990s, a period that also saw the flourishing of a direct-to-video film industry in the former British colonies of Ghana and Nigeria - countries where cinema had until then been hampered by a lack of financial and structural support similar to what France had offered its former colonies.

movies.title: Xala
movies.overview: It is the dawn of Senegal's independence from France, but as the citizens celebrate in the streets we soon become aware that only the faces have changed. White money still controls the government. One official, Aboucader Beye, known by the title "El Hadji," takes advantage of some of that money to marry his third wife, to the sorrow and chagrin of his first two wives and the resentment of his nationalist daughter. But he discovers on his wedding night that he has been struck with a "xala," a curse of impotence. El Hadji goes to comic lengths to find the cause and remove the xala, resulting in a scathing satirical ending.

movies.title: Yeelen
movies.overview: A young man with magical powers journeys to his uncle to request help in fighting his sorcerer father.

movies.title: Chronicle of the Years of Fire
movies.overview: The beginings of the Algerian Revolution as seen through the eyes of a peasant.

movies.title: Touki Bouki
movies.overview: A cowherd with a skull-mounted motorcycle and a university student meet in Dakar; put off by life in Senegal, they plan to make money in Paris.

movies.title: Harvest: 3,000 Years
movies.overview: In this meditative film, the everyday lives of poor Ethiopian peasants are shown using documentary as well as storytelling techniques, and the drama arises out of the timeless but still contemporary issues of their lives.

movies.title: Sarraounia
movies.overview: On 2 January 1899, starting from the French Sudan, a French column under the command of the captains Voulet and Chanoine is sent against the black Sultan Rabah in what is now the Cameroon. Those captains and their African mercenary troops destroy and kill everything they find on their path. The French authorities try to stop them sending orders and a second troop but the captains kill the emissaries who reach them. Sarraounia, queen of the Aznas, have heard about the exactions. Clever in war tactics and in witchcraft, she decides to resist and stop those mad men.

movies.title: Work
movies.overview: A young manager of a factory encounters a man walking along a road who says his family traditionally are servants to the manager's family. The manager offers him a job, and as he watches out for the other man's welfare, begins to see how the company mistreats its workers. The manager is challenged between his ethics and the pressure from others to protect his own interests as dire problems surface at the factory

movies.title: Grandmother
movies.overview: A small African village. The story focuses on Bila, a ten year old boy who befriends an old woman, Sana. Everybody calls her 'Witch' but Bila himself calls her 'Yaaba' (grandmother). When Bila's cousin Nopoko gets sick it is Sana's medicine that saves her.

movies.title: Emitaï
movies.overview: As World War II is going on in Europe, a conflict arises between the French and the Diola-speaking tribe of Africa, prompting the village women to organize their men to sit beneath a tree to pray.

movies.title: Soleil Ô
movies.overview: The film Soleil Ô, shot over four years with a very low budget, tells the story of a black immigrant who makes his way to Paris in search of “his Gaul ancestors”. This manifesto denounces a new form of slavery: the immigrants desperately seek work, a place to live, but find themselves face to face with indifference, rejection, humiliation…until the final call for uprising. “Soleil Ô” is the title of a West Indian song that tells of the pain of the black people from Dahomey (now Benin) who were taken to the Caribbean as slaves.

movies.title: Letter from My Village
movies.overview: Ngor is a young man living in a Senegalese village who wishes to marry Columba. Ongoing drought in the village has affected its crop of groundnuts and as a result, Ngor cannot afford the bride price for Columba. He goes to Senegal's capital city, Dakar, to try to earn more money and is exploited there. He returns to the villagers and shares his experiences of the city with the other men. The story, which shows the daily lives of the villagers, is told in the form of a letter to a friend from a villager, voiced by Faye.

movies.title: God's Gift
movies.overview: In pre-colonial times a peddler crossing the savanna discovers a child lying unconscious in the bush. When the boy comes to, he is mute and cannot explain who he is. The peddler leaves him with a family in the nearest village. After a search for his parents, the family adopts him, giving him the name Wend Kuuni (God's Gift) and a loving sister with whom he bonds. Wend Kuuni regains his speech only after witnessing a tragic event that prompts him to reveal his own painful history.

movies.title: The Choice
movies.overview: Poverty and misery are rife in Gourga, a village in the Sahel. The inhabitants must choose: stay and await international assistance or leave for more fertile regions in the country.

The first blockbuster is released: Jaws; meanwhile, auteur cinema grows with Martin Scorsese and other great directors. The '80s arrive with low-budget productions and era-defining comedies.
